items.title: More young hikers lost using Google Maps on Lake District fells, say rescuers
items.content:
Image source, Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team

Image caption, Three men needed rescuing after they got lost walking from Scafell Pike using Google Maps, which had not updated

By Samantha Jagger North East and Cumbria

More young people are getting caught out on the fells due to relying on Google Maps for navigation, rescuers have said.

After a full-team rescue on Sunday, Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team (WMRT) said an increasing amount of young people, mostly aged 18 to 24, were getting lost or into trouble after using Google Maps on their phones.

WMRT said Google Maps was "not made for the mountains", because unlike a paper map, the app does not display steep rocky outcrops, fell paths and contours, which show three-dimensional shape of the land.

The advice to use a paper map - which is echoed by Google - has been repeated by rescue teams for years, so how can navigation be made more available to young people?

"It's a tricky one," mountaineering and climbing instructor (MCI) Pippa Archer, who lives in Kendal, said.

"I can see the appeal of using something that is free and readily available on your phone, however, a map and compass won't set you back too much," she said.

Archer, who guides and helps people develop their skills in the mountains, said the detail on a paper map was "crucial for staying safe" and "gives a picture of what to expect on your walk, and this is the key to not getting lost".

"A walking map will show you where the ground gets really steep, where there are cliffs to avoid, or streams that need to be crossed," she said.

Image caption, Mountaineering and climbing instructor Pippa Archer said a paper map was "crucial for staying safe"

"The apparent increase in Google Maps use in mountain environments may reflect changing navigation habits rather than simply poor preparation or judgement," winter mountain leader and MCI James Anstee said.

Anstee, who lives in Windermere, said the app's "familiarity and reliability in everyday settings may create an assumption that it is equally suitable for the mountains", without full appreciation of what the terrain demands.

"The challenge is therefore as much about awareness and education as it is about technology," he said.

He said encouraging people to understand limitations of navigation applications, learning about terrain and appropriate navigational competence was "likely to be more beneficial than simply discouraging the use of a particular app".

Image caption, James Anstee says the "challenge is as much about awareness and education as it is about technology"

As a secondary choice for navigation on the phone, WMRT recommended OS Maps, Hiiker or Outdooractive apps which were made for walkers.

Even with the rise of digital devices in recent years, Archer said a compass and a map were still the safest tools, as apps can freeze without signal or could need an update while up on the fell with no phone signal.

It comes as three men needed help on Sunday after they got lost walking from Scafell Pike using Google Maps, which had not updated, rescuers said.

Archer said: "If I used my phone for all my navigation it would quickly run the battery down, compromising my safety if I did need to call for rescue.

"I only use a navigation app for two purposes: to quickly pinpoint my position, or to zoom in to see the map better," she said, and advised people to take screen shots of a map as a back up.

Archer said: "I know some people worry they don't know how to use a compass, but the main thing to remember is that the red end of the needle always points north.

items.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
items.content:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.

A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released.

Grand Theft Auto , or GTA , games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy.

But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6 ’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.

I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.

(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)

I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!

After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull —and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. items.title: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
items.summary: networking
items.content:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

2026-11-15 Oscar Molnar 8 min read (1684 words)

# unifi   Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR . I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable

UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display

UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website , so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control . I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Open Social Web Alliance
items.content:
How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?

The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.

A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on.

The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces.

This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols.

The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill.

For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch?

We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success.

An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there.

As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).

items.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
items.summary: rust
items.content:
This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs , published 4.5 years ago.

The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid.

There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey ), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.

Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology.

GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity.

RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences.

Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.

Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI.

One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework.

It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord.

My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications.

Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away.

Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging.

There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants.

So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases.

But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer.

I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted.

Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold ) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI.

However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025 ) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different.

Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native.

One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right.

In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust.

I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native.

I believe 1Password has this architecture.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

Microsoft has admitted it cannot guarantee data sovereignty for customers in France or other European Union countries under the US Cloud Act, which allows the US government to access data from US-based tech firms, even if that data is stored overseas.

Questioned about legal protections against US access to EU data, Microsoft France reps Anton Carniaux and Pierre Lagarde confirmed the company would analyze and resist any unfounded US data requests, but ultimately, the company is legally obliged to comply with valid ones.

Importantly, the company has never received a US data request for information stored in Europe, according to its transparency reports, however ongoing geopolitical tensions have sovereign nations worried about that.

Microsoft cannot guarantee data sovereignty

Microsoft stressed there are systems in place to minimize data transfers, to keep EU customer data within the EU, but Carniaux acknowledged that he could not guarantee the US wouldn't access French citizen data without French government consent, raising huge concerns.

Earlier this year, the EU Data Boundary for the Microsoft Cloud project was confirmed complete, with other hyperscaler rivals also investing heavily in European sovereignty, but the latest developments have rendered their efforts not worthwhile after all.

Interestingly, AWS, Microsoft and Google all supported the bill when it was passed, so it's not new news to them.

items.title: AI Speeds Up Development - and Accessibility Debt
items.content:
Blog > AI Speeds Up Development – and Accessibility Debt

There’s a problem with the way we talk about productivity gains from AI coding tools: we tend to count the work produced without accounting for the work it creates. Generating a feature quickly is useful. Generating a feature that requires accessibility remediation creates additional work, and that work belongs in any honest assessment of how much time was saved.

For teams that already struggle with accessibility, increasing development speed can increase the rate at which they accumulate accessibility technical debt. If accessibility problems routinely make it through your development process, adding more code to that process gives you more code to evaluate and potentially fix.

Suppose your team doubles the number of features it delivers thanks to AI coding tools. Has its capacity to evaluate accessibility also doubled? Have accessibility requirements become part of the specifications given to the coding agent? Does the agent have access to tested components? Are accessibility checks part of the acceptance criteria? If those things haven’t changed, there’s little reason to assume the additional output will be any more accessible than what the team produced before.

The problems can also spread beyond the original implementation. An agent generates a custom control, a developer approves it, and it becomes the pattern used throughout the application. If that control has an accessibility defect, subsequent features inherit it. Fixing the original component may address part of the problem, but somebody still needs to check the places it was used, particularly where its behavior has been modified or important properties (such as ARIA) have added that didn’t exist before implementation.

This is familiar territory for anyone who has dealt with accessibility remediation. The difference is how quickly the application can grow while those problems remain undiscovered. A team’s accessibility backlog only contains the problems somebody has identified. An unchanged backlog alongside increased development output doesn’t necessarily indicate success. It may indicate that testing hasn’t kept up.

The practical response is to make accessibility part of the work you ask the coding tool to perform and the process you use to accept its output. That means documented interaction requirements, evaluated components, automated testing, and manual verification appropriate to the feature. It also means giving developers enough accessibility knowledge to recognize when generated code needs correction.

A prompt that says “follow WCAG” doesn’t establish that the result meets your requirements. Neither does the agent’s assurance that it has made everything accessible. Those claims need verification, just as they would if a developer made them. AI coding tools can help with that work, too. They can implement corrections, apply an improved pattern across a codebase, and help develop regression tests. Their usefulness depends on the quality of the instructions and the evaluation of the result.

Teams adopting these tools need to account for the entire development process, including the work required to make the output usable. Otherwise, some of the apparent time savings are simply remediation work deferred until later. Users encounter the barriers in the meantime.

items.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
items.content:
I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi

Before I get too deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone else .

Thus, I've finally joined the NTP Pool , offering one public Stratum 2 NTP time server ( ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com ), which gets its time from my Stratum 1 time server ( time.jeffgeerling.com ) in the studio.

My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6 , which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T .

I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:

I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:

You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!

The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:

Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period)

Maintaining a good time—which can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3

A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.

If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.

Your NTP server's IP address will be public

NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even years before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP

The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my website —and was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.

I had to cycle my home IP , then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).

For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:

Stratum 1 : I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to:

Stratum 2 : A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)

I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:

This provides me with the following graph:

I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.

For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here .

The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.

Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time Security —I haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it . I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Entirely human Riemann Hypothesis proof by Alessandro Masullo rushed out hours after Alpöge's AI assisted proof announced
items.content:
For 167 years, nobody could prove the Riemann Hypothesis. On Friday, two separate proofs appeared within hours of each other: one produced with AI, and one, its backers stress, without any AI at all.

The first was the note on Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge’s website . It claims a proof of both the Riemann Hypothesis and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), found working with Claude and released only as Lean code. A few hours later, Ravi Vakil, the Stanford mathematician who is president of the American Mathematical Society, published a short and unusually urgent post on his blog. It announced that another mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, has a proposed proof of GRH.

Vakil’s post reads like it was written in a hurry, and he says so. He explains that he was at a meeting of the AMS Executive Committee and Board of Trustees and about to chair a session lasting several hours, but that the matter was too urgent to wait.

According to Vakil, Masullo’s proposed proof has been under close scrutiny for months by Brian Conrad, the Stanford number theorist widely known for his exacting standards. Conrad has given extensive feedback, Masullo has been working it into the draft, and Vakil says the proof is “so far looking good.” Vakil spells out how it differs from the day’s other claim: “It is all human, with no AI.”

The plan, Vakil writes, had been to bring Masullo to Stanford for a year to polish the write-up, run it past enough experts, and only then announce it. Instead, he decided it was best to release the current draft immediately. He asked the community to check it quickly, formalize it, and fill any small gaps that turn up. He added that he really hopes it works, that he has great faith in Conrad’s judgement, and that there is a long story to tell later.

Vakil’s post doesn’t mention Alpöge or Claude. But it went up a few hours after the AI-assisted claim surfaced, and it explicitly abandons a year-long plan for a careful release. That makes the reason for the rush hard to miss.

Masullo is not a well-known name outside specialist circles. He is a co-author with Conrad of lecture notes on the étale cohomology of number fields, which places him in the same corner of arithmetic geometry where Conrad works. Science journalist Kevin Hartnett wrote that he had been following the story for years and that Masullo “thought he had more time but didn’t.”

This is massive. A story I've been following for years. He thought he had more time but didn't. Alessandro Masullo announces a separate, purely human proof of the Riemann hypothesis. https://t.co/XHMLOFNq8y

— Kevin Hartnett (@KSHartnett) November 20, 2026

Two proofs, two very different kinds of evidence

If both claims hold up, the most famous open problem in mathematics will have been solved twice on the same day. The two releases could hardly be more different, though.

Alpöge’s claim comes with no human-readable proof. The note says a written-out version would run past 250,000 pages, so only the Lean formalization has been released. Its strength is that a machine can check it. Mathematician Elliot Glazer said early on that the formal statement in Alpöge’s code is GRH, and Scientific American has since reported that MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland independently compiled the Lean code. A successful compile still has to be backed up by experts confirming that the definitions are right and that no hidden assumptions slipped in. But it is the kind of verification that can come quickly. What the Lean-only release doesn’t offer is understanding. As mathematicians reacting to the claim have noted , even its author describes parts of it as beyond his own expertise.

Masullo’s proof is the opposite. It is a traditional human argument, written to be read, and it has already had months of attention from one of the most careful checkers in number theory. But it hasn’t been formalized, it is still an unpolished draft, and its main endorsement so far is Conrad’s private review,…
